# Investigative Report: Attribution Chain Linking Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks to GRU Election-Interference Operations

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports the conclusion that **Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks were not independent Romanian or American hacktivist personas, but elements of a coordinated GRU-controlled operation** that stole political documents and released them to influence the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The strongest evidence is the July 2018 federal indictment, which attributes the personas, infrastructure, financing, malware, and release activity to named officers of GRU Units 26165 and 74455. CrowdStrike’s incident-response account independently identified a Russian-affiliated intrusion into the Democratic National Committee (DNC), including the use of X-Agent and X-Tunnel malware associated with the actor CrowdStrike called FANCY BEAR. The two sources align on the technical infrastructure, malware, timing, and separation between intrusion activity and public dissemination. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The evidence should nevertheless be characterized accurately. The indictment contains **criminal allegations**, not convictions. It identifies the alleged operators and describes evidence available to the grand jury, but the defendants were not tried in the United States on the basis of the material supplied here. CrowdStrike’s article is an incident-response and threat-intelligence account produced by a commercial cybersecurity company retained by the DNC; it is important corroborating evidence, but it is not itself a judicial finding. The appropriate conclusion is therefore that the public evidence establishes a **high-confidence attribution assessment**, rather than a claim that every allegation has been adjudicated in court. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## Sources and evidentiary roles

For this report, the duplicated source material is consolidated into two source IDs:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | U.S. Department of Justice indictment, July 13, 2018 | Alleged criminal attribution, named GRU officers, operational chronology, persona activity, infrastructure, cryptocurrency payments, document transfers, and election-system targeting |
| **S2** | CrowdStrike, “Bears in the Midst: Intrusion Into the Democratic National Committee,” with 2020 update | Incident-response observations, malware and actor attribution, DNC timeline, exfiltration qualification, and response to claims concerning the DNC investigation |

S1 is the most probative source for the specific Guccifer 2.0/DCLeaks attribution chain because it connects named individuals and GRU units to domains, accounts, servers, malware, Bitcoin transactions, and dissemination activity. S2 is especially valuable as an independent technical chronology of the DNC intrusion and as corroboration that the malware and methods described in the indictment were observed during the real-world incident. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## The narrative under investigation

### The public personas

The indictment alleges that the conspirators created and operated two principal online identities:

1. **DCLeaks**, presented publicly as the work of “American hacktivists”; and  
2. **Guccifer 2.0**, presented publicly as a lone Romanian hacker.

According to S1, both descriptions were false. The indictment alleges that GRU officers created the personas to release stolen material while concealing the Russian government’s role. The alleged operation began with credential theft and network intrusion, proceeded through document collection and exfiltration, and culminated in staged online releases. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The narrative is significant because the personas served different but complementary purposes. DCLeaks provided a front for publishing stolen emails and documents, while Guccifer 2.0 claimed personal responsibility for the DNC intrusion and interacted with journalists, political actors, and an organization that later published large quantities of the stolen material. The indictment treats this not as spontaneous activity by unrelated individuals, but as a coordinated dissemination architecture operated by GRU personnel. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### The underlying intrusion

S1 alleges that GRU Unit 26165 conducted the core hacking operations. The indictment assigns Unit 26165 responsibility for the DCCC and DNC intrusions and for targeting individuals associated with Hillary Clinton’s campaign. It describes spearphishing beginning no later than March 2016, including a March 19 email directed to the Clinton campaign chairman. The resulting compromise allegedly enabled the theft of more than 50,000 emails from that account. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment further alleges that the conspirators compromised the DCCC in April 2016, installed X-Agent malware on at least ten DCCC computers, monitored keystrokes and screenshots, and transmitted information to a GRU-leased server in Arizona referred to as the “AMS” panel. The conspirators allegedly used X-Tunnel to move compressed stolen documents through encrypted channels to GRU-leased infrastructure, including a server in Illinois. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment alleges that the DNC was then accessed through stolen credentials obtained from the DCCC. By June 2016, the conspirators allegedly had access to approximately 33 DNC computers. They searched for election-related information, including opposition research and files associated with Hillary Clinton, Ted Cruz, and Donald Trump. The alleged operators also cleared event logs, attempted to remove traces with CCleaner, and maintained access despite remediation efforts. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

CrowdStrike’s account broadly corroborates this technical sequence. CrowdStrike reported that it was engaged by the DNC on April 30, 2016, began its investigation on May 1, and identified two separate adversaries: COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR. It associated FANCY BEAR with X-Agent and X-Tunnel, while describing the DNC’s FANCY BEAR intrusion as beginning in April 2016. ([CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## The attribution chain

### 1. GRU unit and personnel attribution

S1 identifies Unit 26165 and Unit 74455 as GRU units involved in cyber operations and staged document releases. Viktor Netyksho is alleged to have commanded Unit 26165. Boris Antonov and Dmitriy Badin are alleged to have supervised targeting operations. Ivan Yermakov is alleged to have participated in email and DNC server intrusions, while Aleksey Lukashev is alleged to have sent spearphishing emails to Clinton campaign personnel. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment assigns malware development and monitoring responsibilities to Sergey Morgachev, Nikolay Kozachek, Pavel Yershov, and Artem Malyshev. It separately assigns release and infrastructure responsibilities to Unit 74455 officers Aleksandr Osadchuk and Aleksey Potemkin. Anatoliy Kovalev is alleged to have participated in separate attacks on state election-administration systems. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This division of labor is analytically important. It describes a structured operation with separate functions for spearphishing, malware development, network access, data theft, infrastructure administration, persona operation, and public release. That structure is inconsistent with the explanation that Guccifer 2.0 was simply an unaffiliated individual acting alone. The latter explanation is an alleged cover story in the indictment, not a supported attribution finding. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### 2. Persona creation and timing

S1 alleges that DCLeaks was constructed before the public release of documents. On April 19, 2016, the conspirators allegedly registered the dcleaks.com domain through an anonymizing service, using funds connected to cryptocurrency accounts and an operational email account. The website was launched on June 8, 2016, and presented itself as the work of American hacktivists. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment alleges that Guccifer 2.0 was created immediately after the DNC publicly announced on June 14, 2016, that Russian government actors had hacked its network. On June 15, an operator allegedly logged into a Moscow-based server managed by Unit 74455 and searched for English phrases that appeared in Guccifer 2.0’s first blog post later that day. The timing and phrase overlap are presented as evidence that the persona was created to counter the attribution to Russia. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### 3. Shared infrastructure and financing

The strongest bridge between DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 is the alleged overlap in infrastructure and financing. S1 states that both operations used overlapping computer infrastructure and funding. The same pool of Bitcoin funds allegedly purchased a VPN account and a Malaysian server. The VPN was later used to access the @Guccifer_2 Twitter account, while the Malaysian server hosted the DCLeaks website. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment also alleges that the same server infrastructure was used to register malicious domains connected to the DNC and DCCC intrusions. It describes hundreds of email accounts, fictitious names and addresses, cryptocurrency mining, peer-to-peer purchases, digital-currency layering, and payments for servers and domains. The alleged purpose was to obscure the operators’ identities and their links to Russia and the Russian government. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### 4. Direct connection to stolen material

S1 alleges that Guccifer 2.0 transferred stolen material to journalists, a state lobbyist and political-news source, and Organization 1. In one alleged transfer, approximately 2.5 gigabytes of DCCC data—including donor records and personal identifying information for more than 2,000 Democratic donors—were provided to a U.S. recipient. In another, Guccifer 2.0 sent stolen documents concerning the Black Lives Matter movement to a reporter. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment alleges that Guccifer 2.0 also communicated with a U.S. person who was regularly in contact with senior members of Donald J. Trump’s campaign. The messages asked whether the recipient found anything interesting in posted documents and offered further assistance. S1 does not, in the supplied text, allege that the recipient knowingly coordinated with Russian intelligence or that the campaign itself directed the hacking. The evidence supports a claim about outreach by the Guccifer 2.0 persona, not a broader unsupported claim about campaign culpability. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

### 5. Transfer to Organization 1 and staged publication

S1 alleges that Guccifer 2.0 discussed release timing with Organization 1. Organization 1 allegedly requested new DNC material before the Democratic National Convention because it would have greater impact. The conspirators allegedly sent encrypted instructions on July 14, 2016, and Organization 1 confirmed receipt of an archive of approximately one gigabyte. On July 22, Organization 1 released more than 20,000 DNC emails and documents, approximately three days before the convention. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment further alleges that Organization 1 released approximately 33 tranches of documents from the Clinton campaign chairman between October 7 and November 7, 2016, totaling more than 50,000 stolen documents. This alleged coordination establishes the dissemination stage of the operation: stolen data was not merely published indiscriminately, but was selected and timed for political effect. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

## Comparison of the competing explanations

| Issue | Guccifer 2.0/DCLeaks cover narrative | Evidence-supported explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Lone Romanian hacker or American hacktivists | GRU-operated personas, according to the indictment |
| Relationship to DNC hack | Independent claim of responsibility | Persona activity followed and responded to public disclosure of the DNC intrusion |
| Infrastructure | No stated relationship between personas | Shared VPN, server, domain-registration, and Bitcoin infrastructure alleged |
| Malware | Not explained by persona narrative | X-Agent and X-Tunnel linked to the intrusion and to GRU Unit 26165 |
| Release process | Independent online publication | Coordinated transfer, timing, and staged publication alleged |
| Russian connection | Denied by Guccifer 2.0 | Indictment alleges Moscow-based Unit 74455 infrastructure and Russian military officers |

The alternative narrative fails to explain the combined evidence. It does not account for the alleged shared funding pool, shared VPN and server use, Moscow-based Unit 74455 access, or the connection between the personas and stolen files obtained through the DCCC/DNC intrusions. It also does not explain why Guccifer 2.0’s first post allegedly incorporated phrases searched on a Unit 74455 server shortly beforehand. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

## Incident-response evidence and its limits

CrowdStrike’s evidence is consistent with the indictment in several important respects. CrowdStrike reported that it found two adversaries in the DNC network, identified FANCY BEAR with X-Agent and X-Tunnel, observed a separate April 2016 breach, and concluded that the activity was consistent with Russian intelligence. Its account also describes X-Agent capabilities including remote command execution, file transmission, and keylogging, as well as anti-forensic activity such as event-log clearing and timestamp manipulation. ([CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

However, CrowdStrike expressly qualified the exfiltration evidence. Shawn Henry’s testimony, quoted in S2, stated that CrowdStrike had indicators and circumstantial evidence that data left the network, but did not have a network sensor that directly observed the transfer in real time. This limitation does not negate the broader attribution, but it means the specific technical evidence should not be overstated as direct observation of every exfiltration event. ([CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The indictment supplies additional evidence beyond CrowdStrike’s initial investigation, including alleged server leases, domain registrations, cryptocurrency transactions, persona communications, and transfers to Organization 1. Thus, the two sources have different evidentiary scopes: CrowdStrike documents the intrusion and malware; S1 presents the government’s broader attribution theory connecting intrusion, financing, personas, and dissemination. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## Contradictions and uncertainty

There is no material contradiction between S1 and S2 regarding the central attribution chain. Both associate the DNC intrusion with Russian intelligence-linked activity and identify X-Agent/X-Tunnel tradecraft. The principal difference is one of emphasis and evidentiary qualification: S1 alleges completed theft and attribution to specific GRU officers, while S2 states that CrowdStrike did not directly observe all data leaving the network in real time. That is a limitation on the form of evidence, not a contradiction in the overall conclusion. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The largest uncertainty is legal rather than technical. The supplied S1 document is an indictment and therefore states allegations returned by a grand jury. It should not be described as a conviction or final judicial determination. The attribution assessment is nevertheless strong because the indictment provides multiple mutually reinforcing indicators: named GRU officers, unit assignments, malware roles, operational accounts, domains, servers, cryptocurrency transactions, persona behavior, and publication coordination. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

## Conclusion

Based solely on S1 and S2, the most defensible conclusion is that **Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks were operational personas within a GRU-linked election-interference campaign**. The attribution does not depend on a single indicator. It rests on a cumulative chain:

1. A Russian military-intelligence organization is alleged to have conducted the intrusions.
2. Unit 26165 is linked to spearphishing, DCCC/DNC access, X-Agent, X-Tunnel, and document theft.
3. Unit 74455 is linked to infrastructure, social-media activity, and document-release support.
4. DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 are alleged to have been created and operated by the same broader GRU apparatus.
5. The personas used overlapping infrastructure and Bitcoin financing.
6. Guccifer 2.0 distributed stolen material obtained through the DCCC/DNC intrusions.
7. The stolen material was allegedly transferred to Organization 1 with discussions about timing and political impact.
8. CrowdStrike’s technical findings independently align with the indictment’s description of the DNC intrusion and malware.

The “lone Romanian hacker” and “American hacktivist” explanations are therefore best assessed as **cover narratives**, not credible alternative explanations of the total evidence. The conclusion remains an attribution assessment supported by a criminal indictment and incident-response evidence, not a statement that every allegation was adjudicated through a completed trial. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election); [CrowdStrike, 2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

## References

CrowdStrike. (2020, June 4). *CrowdStrike’s work with the Democratic National Committee: Setting the record straight*. CrowdStrike. [https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

U.S. Department of Justice. (2018, July 13). *Grand jury indicts 12 Russian intelligence officers for hacking offenses related to the 2016 election*. [https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
